provenance.source_identity: William Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution, 2002 edition; IndexerLabs-derived body-text PDF missing front matter and endnotes
provenance.discovery_method: Fresh candidate-blind source-led review of every owned page and all declared context pages under subject-index-standard-policy-v1. Earlier discoveries were not inspected before this draft was complete.

chunk.title: 6. The Breakdown of the Revolutionary Consensus, 1790–1791
chapter_labels: The Breakdown of the Revolutionary Consensus, 1790–1791

word_count_methodology.included: All indexable chapter body prose, including displayed block quotations.
word_count_methodology.excluded: Running heads, page numbers, the chapter display title, blank matter, and footnote reference numerals; unavailable endnote text was not counted.
word_count_methodology.extraction_and_tokenization: Text layer reviewed page by page; line-end hyphenation was rejoined before Unicode word-token counting. Hyphenated lexical compounds count as one token.
word_count_methodology.density_role: Denominator metadata only; it was not used to set, prune, or pad the subject count.

excluded_regions.description: Running chapter heads and printed page numbers were excluded from discovery and word count.
Chapter number, title display, and date subtitle were treated as navigation furniture rather than indexable prose.

unavailable_regions.effect: Superscript note calls were visible, but note text could not be reviewed or counted.

reader_tasks.reader_question: Explain why the broad revolutionary consensus of 1790 disintegrated by the end of the Constituent Assembly.
Trace the sequence from early Church reforms through the Civil Constitution, clerical oath, and breach with Rome.
Compare constitutional and refractory clergy and explain the regional and social pattern of oath-taking.
Explain how Catholic–Protestant conflict, papal policy, and Avignon connected religion to counter-revolution.
Assess how political clubs mobilized opinion and changed alignment during the religious and Varennes crises.
Explain how religious conflict gave counter-revolution a popular base beyond émigré elites.
Trace Louis XVI’s alienation from the Revolution and the planning, failure, and political meaning of Varennes.
Explain why the Assembly retained the monarchy after Varennes despite evidence of the king’s repudiation.
Trace the emergence of republican politics from Varennes through the Jacobin split and Champ de Mars.
Assess Lafayette, the National Guard, and Paris popular mobilization in the spring and summer of 1791.
Explain the economic and labor setting of the Le Chapelier Law and its long-term restriction of worker organization.
Trace the political moderation of Barnave, Duport, the Lameths, and the formation and failure of the Feuillants.
Explain Robespierre’s rise, his procedural victories, and his positions on colonial and constitutional questions.
Analyze the Assembly’s treatment of slavery and political rights for free people of color in Saint-Domingue.
Connect army disorder, officer and noble emigration, foreign intervention fears, and the Declaration of Pillnitz.
Evaluate the achievements, exclusions, internal contradictions, and viability of the Constitution of 1791.

subjects.label: Breakdown of the revolutionary consensus, 1790–1791
subjects.meaning: The chapter’s governing explanation of how a broadly supported reform settlement fractured into religious, royalist, republican, social, and international antagonisms.
subjects.stance: The author treats the collapse as cumulative but assigns exceptional causal weight to the Assembly’s coercive religious policy and the king’s attempted flight.

relationships.description: The clerical oath forced a public alignment for or against the new order.
Varennes exposed the king’s repudiation and forced a second national choice.
Champ de Mars turned political division into lethal repression.
The Feuillant settlement lacked a durable constituency.

evidence.evidence_summary: The opening contrasts clerical goodwill in 1789 with rapidly accumulating losses and distrust as the Revolution transformed the Church.
The chapter’s synthesis attributes national division chiefly to the clerical oath, papal rupture, royal estrangement, Varennes, and the monarchist–republican split.
The closing judgment presents the constitutional settlement as politically friendless and therefore unlikely to endure.

subjects.label: Clergy’s revolutionary role and reform expectations in 1789
subjects.meaning: Clerical deputies initially helped transform the Estates-General while expecting reform, not destruction of the clergy’s corporate status or autonomy.
subjects.stance: The author rejects hindsight: early clerical cooperation did not constitute consent to the far-reaching ecclesiastical settlement that followed.

relationships.description: Initial cooperation gave way to material and institutional losses.
The later Civil Constitution went beyond the reform mandate many clerics believed they had accepted.

evidence.evidence_summary: Clerical deputies are shown breaking the privileged orders’ deadlock for humanitarian and political reasons while retaining corporate expectations.
The cahiers anticipated rational religious reform but not surrender of the clergy’s separate status or protective authority.

subjects.label: Clerical losses, Church property, and state dependence
subjects.meaning: The abolition of tithes, dues, pluralism, and papal payments, followed by nationalization of Church property, removed the clergy’s independent material base and made it dependent on state salaries.
subjects.stance: The author presents these measures as a sequence of losses that turned much clerical enthusiasm into a sense of dispossession despite promised income and public functions.

relationships.description: Loss of the Church’s independent resources made comprehensive state reorganization increasingly likely.
Closures contributed to Paris unemployment and social distress.

evidence.evidence_summary: The August decrees removed tithes, vestry fees, pluralism, ecclesiastical dues, and payments to Rome, often without effective compensation.
Confiscation of Church estates, uncertain salary payments, and collapsing tithe collection left many priests viewing reform as dispossession plus promises.
Inventories and impending sales of Church lands made the new religious order immediately visible across France.

subjects.label: Catholic establishment, religious liberty, and civil equality
subjects.meaning: Revolutionary rights policy refused Catholic monopoly or state-religion status while extending public office and civil rights beyond Catholics.
subjects.stance: The author treats these measures as principled revolutionary changes that also deepened clerical and Catholic fears of a Protestant or anti-Catholic transformation.

relationships.description: Dom Gerle’s motion sought formal Catholic monopoly.
Religious equality became entangled with local struggles for political power.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Declaration’s settlement withheld official Catholic status, protected opinion, and opened civil rights and office to Protestants and Jews.
Dom Gerle’s attempt to restore Catholic monopoly drew substantial support but failed in an Assembly led at the time by a Protestant president.
Catholic suspicions intensified where Protestant minorities rapidly acquired political and military influence.

subjects.label: Dissolution of monasteries and convents
subjects.meaning: The Assembly dissolved most regular religious houses and prohibited new vows, retaining only institutions serving education or charity.
subjects.stance: The author explains the policy through Enlightenment utility and recent reform precedent while stressing that Catholics perceived it as another element of a hostile pattern.

relationships.description: Institutional suppression followed loss of religious property and income.
The dissolution expressed the state’s functional conception of the national Church.

evidence.evidence_summary: Most monasteries and convents were dissolved after losing their property; contemplative life was judged socially unproductive.
Joseph II’s reforms and earlier French closures supplied precedents, but the cumulative attack on Church institutions made the measure more alarming.

subjects.label: Dom Gerle’s national-religion motion
subjects.meaning: A clerical deputy’s April 1790 proposal sought to declare Catholicism the national religion and grant it exclusive public worship.
subjects.stance: The episode is treated as a revealing but defeated attempt to halt religious pluralization, not as the Assembly’s governing policy.

relationships.description: The motion opposed the religious equality embedded in the revolutionary rights settlement.
Clubs at Bergerac and Tulle formed in opposition to deputies who supported the motion.

evidence.evidence_summary: Dom Gerle’s motion attracted roughly three hundred votes but failed, dramatizing the Assembly’s refusal to restore Catholic monopoly.

boundaries_and_exclusions: Do not turn Dom Gerle’s personal biography into an independent subject beyond this policy intervention.

subjects.label: Protestant political ascendancy and Catholic reaction in Nîmes and Montauban
subjects.meaning: Economic strength, electoral organization, and militia control gave Protestant minorities sudden political influence, prompting Catholic municipal mobilization and mutual exclusion.
subjects.stance: The author rejects a purely theological account: sectarian violence grew from a rapid redistribution of local political and coercive power.

relationships.description: Montauban’s struggle over inventories and militia control became lethal.
Nîmes electoral and militia conflict culminated in the bagarre.
Defeated Catholic leaders later redirected grievances into the Jalès movement.

evidence.evidence_summary: Organized Protestant bourgeois groups captured representation and militia influence in Nîmes and Montauban, while Catholics mobilized municipal majorities.
Catholics in the Gard came to identify revolutionary government with a feared Protestant victory and inversion of the local order.

subjects.label: Montauban riot of May 1790
subjects.meaning: Catholic crowds stopped inventories of confiscated monastic property and attacked a Protestant-linked militia, producing deaths and Protestant flight.
subjects.stance: The author treats the riot as an early fusion of religious grievance, Church-property policy, and control of local armed power.

relationships.description: The riot grew from the local Catholic–Protestant power struggle.
Women also formed a conspicuous part of later Parisian popular mobilization, though in a different political setting.

evidence.evidence_summary: A crowd led prominently by devout women blocked monastic inventories, overwhelmed the militia, killed five, and drove frightened Protestants from the city.
Order returned only after nonsectarian militia forces from Bordeaux intervened.

subjects.label: Bagarre de Nîmes and the Gard power settlement
subjects.meaning: Four days of armed sectarian conflict ended in a Protestant victory, heavy Catholic deaths, and Protestant control of city and departmental institutions.
subjects.stance: The author characterizes the bagarre as a massacre rather than a minor brawl and makes its political aftermath central to Catholic counter-revolutionary grievance.

relationships.description: The bagarre resolved the immediate local power struggle in Protestant favor.
Defeated Catholic leaders carried their grievances into the Jalès federation.

evidence.evidence_summary: Electoral tension and rival National Guard companies triggered pitched fighting; Protestant forces prevailed with much heavier Catholic losses.
Subsequent Protestant electoral victories made them agents of revolutionary and ecclesiastical policy throughout the Gard.

subjects.label: Avignon and the Comtat Venaissin: annexation and civil conflict
subjects.meaning: Papal subjects divided over union with France; annexationists seized municipal power and proclaimed union, while anti-annexation and papal resistance produced prolonged civil war before the Assembly annexed the territories.
subjects.stance: The author distinguishes genuine popular annexationism from contested sovereignty and emphasizes the issue’s international and religious consequences.

relationships.description: The territorial dispute aggravated the breach with Pius VI.
Annexationists used club affiliation to signal alignment with revolutionary France.
Annexation compounded the religious split in the chapter’s closing assessment.

evidence.evidence_summary: Annexationists in Avignon aligned local law with French reforms, defeated papal loyalists with French National Guard help, and proclaimed union.
The Comtat remained divided and experienced a year of civil war, making claims of settled popular will untenable.
Robespierre’s unsuccessful demand for immediate annexation marked another fracture on the left.
The Constituent Assembly finally annexed Avignon and the Comtat as a defiant final act amid foreign-war rumors.

subjects.label: Pius VI and the breach between Rome and revolutionary France
subjects.meaning: Pius VI rejected revolutionary religious policy, resisted changes in his enclaves, warned of schism, and ultimately opposed the clerical oath; public disclosure of his position completed the institutional breach.
subjects.stance: The author presents papal silence as tactical delay rather than acceptance and distinguishes early private condemnation from the later public rupture.

relationships.description: The Civil Constitution displaced papal authority in French Church governance.
Publication of the papal position led some sworn clergy to retract.
The breach supplied counter-revolution with a religious cause.

evidence.evidence_summary: Pius VI rejected annexationist reforms in Avignon and privately condemned the Declaration of Rights and French religious policy.
He urged Louis XVI against sanctioning the Civil Constitution as schismatic, then delayed publicly while consulting and seeking to avoid an immediate break.
Papal letters against the Civil Constitution and oath became public, oath withdrawals followed, the nuncio departed, and the breach was complete.

subjects.label: Civil Constitution of the Clergy
subjects.meaning: The July 1790 settlement reconstructed the French Church as a salaried, territorially rationalized, electorally staffed national institution subordinated in temporal organization to the revolutionary state.
subjects.stance: The author sees many administrative reforms as defensible and acceptable, but identifies unilateral state action, lay election, and papal displacement as the provisions that made schism likely.

relationships.description: State control followed removal of the Church’s independent material base.
Administrative rationalization was its broadly acceptable component.
Lay election and Richerist echoes were its contentious appointment component.
Resistance to implementation led the Assembly to impose the clerical oath.

evidence.evidence_summary: The ecclesiastical committee aimed to revitalize and financially stabilize the Church while harmonizing it with revolutionary principles.
The Assembly adopted the plan with little amendment, combining salary, residence, diocesan, parish, and benefice reforms.
Lay election of clergy and reduction of papal confirmation to notification created the deepest canonical objections.
Enforcement, episcopal elections, and resistance showed that transition would not be consensual.
The settlement was later excluded from the Constitution, leaving it amendable as ordinary law and separating a constitutional oath from acceptance of the ecclesiastical order.

subjects.label: Ecclesiastical Committee and national-Church sovereignty
subjects.meaning: A lay-dominated Assembly committee pursued a leaner Church modeled rhetorically on early-Christian discipline and denied the Pope authority over France’s temporal religious organization.
subjects.stance: The author notes that only a minority were freethinking anti-clericals; most reformers understood themselves as sincere Catholics, which makes the ensuing conflict more than a simple secular assault.

relationships.description: The committee prepared the Civil Constitution.
Its sovereignty claim underlay termination of the Concordat and rejection of a national council.

evidence.evidence_summary: When clerical committee members slowed, lay membership was expanded; most participants sought Catholic reform rather than destruction of religion.
The committee distinguished papal spiritual authority from what it regarded as France’s sovereign power to organize religious practice.

subjects.label: Concordat of 1516, national council, and unilateral ecclesiastical reform
subjects.meaning: The Assembly wound up the Concordat without replacement and rejected episcopal requests for a national council to consent to reform.
subjects.stance: The author treats rejection of ecclesiastical consultation as a crucial procedural error: it left no French Church authority capable of offsetting a papal condemnation.

relationships.description: The policy followed the Assembly’s claim to national control over temporal Church organization.
Eliminating a national council made papal opposition harder to mediate.

evidence.evidence_summary: The king was directed to end the Concordat, and no successor agreement with Rome was planned.
Bishops’ proposal for a national council was rejected as revival of a separate clerical order, despite the risk that only the Pope could then speak authoritatively.

subjects.label: Administrative rationalization under the Civil Constitution
subjects.meaning: The Civil Constitution reduced dioceses and parishes, abolished nonpastoral benefices, imposed residence and service requirements, and established public salary scales.
subjects.stance: The author distinguishes these practical reforms from the appointment and papal questions, judging much of the rationalization reasonable and potentially acceptable to most clergy.

relationships.description: These measures formed the less controversial core of the Civil Constitution.
Appointment by lay election created more serious objections.

evidence.evidence_summary: The settlement provided generous though redistributive salaries, strict residence, one bishop per department, fewer parishes, and abolition of chapters and nonpastoral benefices.
Most administrative changes are judged plausible improvements; unemployment from suppressed benefices was the principal immediate cost.

subjects.label: Election of clergy, Richerism, and lay participation
subjects.meaning: Bishops and parish priests were to be elected through secular citizen assemblies, while episcopal advisory councils echoed Richerist calls for less hierarchical Church government.
subjects.stance: The author stresses that clerical reform traditions did not entail election by lay bodies that might include non-Catholics or unbelievers.
acceptable_access: lay election of bishops and priests
anticipated_reader_lookup_routes: lay election of bishops and priests

relationships.description: Lay election was a central institutional feature of the Civil Constitution.
The appointment provisions made canonical acceptance especially difficult.

evidence.evidence_summary: The law assigned episcopal and parish elections to departmental and district assemblies of lay active citizens.
Richerist precedents supported election and synodal advice but not unrestricted lay selection, which raised concerns over spiritual competence.

subjects.label: Papal authority, episcopal appointment, and danger of schism
subjects.meaning: The Civil Constitution prohibited ordinary ties to foreign bishops and reduced papal confirmation of French bishops to notification, while French clerics sought a papal response that might preserve communion.
subjects.stance: The author treats schism as foreseeable but not initially desired by most French clergy or even by the temporizing Pope.

relationships.description: The Civil Constitution’s papal and appointment provisions created the schism problem.
Rejection of a national council removed an alternative source of Church consent.
The later papal letters turned uncertainty into open rupture.

evidence.evidence_summary: The law severed administrative contact with foreign bishops and stripped papal confirmation from appointments while formally retaining spiritual communion.
Clerical deputies and bishops pressed Rome for accommodation, but papal silence left them unable to certify the law’s ecclesiastical legitimacy.

subjects.label: Religion, the press, and political polarization
subjects.meaning: Religious policy became a loyalty test and reorganized public debate as conservative and patriotic newspapers adopted opposing, increasingly anti-clerical or confessional positions.
subjects.stance: The author treats religion as a principal accelerator of polarization rather than a secondary cultural issue.

relationships.description: Religious conflict supplied repeated occasions for club foundation and mobilization.
The loyalty-test dynamic broke the earlier broad coalition.

evidence.evidence_summary: Church-property enforcement and support for the Civil Constitution were framed as measures of loyalty to the Revolution.
Conservative papers coordinated against the Civil Constitution, while patriotic papers answered with forceful anti-clericalism.

subjects.label: Jacobin clubs: growth, affiliation, and political functions
subjects.meaning: The Paris Society of the Friends of the Constitution and its provincial affiliates formed a rapidly expanding national political network that debated policy, sustained enthusiasm, pressured authorities, and circulated patriotic information.
subjects.stance: The author emphasizes pre-revolutionary associational habits and issue-driven local formation, with religion as a leading stimulus.
acceptable_access: Society of the Friends of the Constitution
anticipated_reader_lookup_routes: Society of the Friends of the Constitution

relationships.description: Religious controversy supplied organizing issues.
Midi clubs opposed Catholic counter-revolutionary formations.
Varennes and the king’s reinstatement split the network’s political purposes.
The Feuillant secession divided the Paris mother society.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Paris club evolved from the Breton and Revolution clubs, while affiliates rose from a few dozen to more than two hundred during 1790.
Clubs organized festivals, pressed local officials, distributed papers, exchanged addresses, and trained future revolutionary leaders.
Religious disputes, sectarian clashes, Avignon annexation, and counter-revolutionary alarms energized clubs in the Midi.
The oath crisis expanded the network to more than nine hundred affiliates before Varennes exposed disagreement over monarchy and republicanism.

subjects.label: Camps of Jalès and Catholic armed counter-revolution
subjects.meaning: A National Guard federation in the Gard was redirected by defeated Catholic leaders into organized resistance linked to émigré royalists; a second camp failed militarily.
subjects.stance: The author identifies Jalès as the first armed demonstration openly claiming counter-revolutionary purpose, rooted in sectarian power grievances rather than simple aristocratic restoration.

relationships.description: The Protestant victory at Nîmes furnished Jalès’s leadership and grievances.
The movement coordinated with Artois’s émigré network.
Religious identity helped counter-revolution reach beyond court exiles.

evidence.evidence_summary: Catholic leaders from Nîmes took over a Guard federation, denounced Protestant control, preserved an organizing committee, and contacted Artois’s agents.
A second camp failed to rally decisive forces and was bloodily dispersed by a largely Protestant force.

subjects.label: Exposition of Principles and clerical resistance to enforcement
subjects.meaning: Bishops who opposed the Civil Constitution defended ecclesiastical consultation, while local authorities enforced the law through expulsions, dissolutions, elections, dismissal, and salary suspension.
subjects.stance: The author distinguishes the bishops’ restrained constitutional argument from the insurrectionary meaning attributed to it by patriots.

relationships.description: The Exposition challenged the Civil Constitution’s mode of enactment.
Enforcement difficulties prompted the Assembly to impose a decisive oath.

evidence.evidence_summary: Thirty bishops explained that radical reform required a council or papal consultation, without issuing a call to revolt.
Authorities and clubs nevertheless treated opposition as disobedience, expelled or dismissed bishops, dissolved chapters, held elections, and stopped clerical salaries.
Refusal of confirmation and mass priestly protest showed that a peaceful institutional transition was not occurring.

subjects.label: Clerical oath of 27 November 1790
subjects.meaning: Beneficed clergy were required publicly to swear fidelity to nation, king, law, and the Assembly’s constitution, with refusal bringing replacement under the Civil Constitution.
subjects.stance: The author calls the oath one of the Revolution’s great turning points and the Constituent Assembly’s gravest error because it compelled public choice, legitimized dissent, and divided roughly half the clergy.

relationships.description: The oath was the Assembly’s response to resistance and failed enforcement.
It divided the clergy into constitutional and refractory camps.
Its local outcome registered wider judgments about the Revolution.
It gave opponents a cause extending beyond self-interest.

evidence.evidence_summary: The decree required a public post-Mass oath and immediate replacement of clerics who refused.
The oath is judged a major turning point because coercive identification of dissent also recognized and legitimized refusal.
The Assembly’s clergy split sharply, popular pressure intensified, and about half the national clergy ultimately could not subscribe.
The final assessment makes the forced choice between Church and state a principal cause of national division and popular counter-revolution.

subjects.label: Geography and social determinants of clerical oath-taking
subjects.meaning: Oath-taking varied sharply by region according to clerical economy, cultural distance, earlier anti-episcopal activism, local political pressure, and ties between parish priests and communities.
subjects.stance: The author rejects a single material explanation and gives exceptional importance to lay pressure and local solidarity.

relationships.description: The national division created by the oath had a strongly regional form.
Clerical decisions often mirrored community attitudes toward the Revolution as a whole.

evidence.evidence_summary: High acceptance around Paris and in the southeast contrasted with low rates in culturally distinct borderlands, Protestant-conflict regions, and especially the west.
Western priests’ local peasant origins and parish solidarity mattered at least as much as tithe income, while clubs and authorities shaped outcomes elsewhere.

subjects.label: Clerical oath as a political opinion poll
subjects.meaning: A priest’s oath or refusal frequently expressed parish opinion on the Revolution far beyond ecclesiastical organization; the overall result indicated a large constituency that believed change had gone far enough.
subjects.stance: The author treats the oath as a proxy for wider political consent, not merely a test of clerical doctrine or income.

relationships.description: The oath’s consequences reached beyond the institutional Church.
It made the erosion of consensus publicly measurable.

evidence.evidence_summary: Local lay pressure made clerical choice a broad referendum on revolutionary achievements rather than a narrowly canonical decision.
With about 54 percent of parish clergy swearing, the author infers that more than a third of France was prepared to signal a limit to further Revolution.

subjects.label: Constitutional and refractory clergy: staffing the new Church
subjects.meaning: The oath opened episcopal and parish careers to sworn clergy, former regulars, and previously excluded talent, while widespread refusal produced vacancies, shortages, and temporary reliance on nonjurors.
subjects.stance: The author presents the constitutional Church as both socially mobile and operationally compromised from its inception.

relationships.description: The oath defined the two clerical camps.
Papal intervention induced withdrawals and confirmed the rupture.

evidence.evidence_summary: Nearly the entire episcopate refused, while Talleyrand enabled consecration and the new Church opened advancement to sworn clergy and former regulars.
Vacancies exceeded available replacements, forcing the Assembly to retain refractory clergy temporarily.
Publication of the papal position caused a further group of constitutional clergy to retract their oaths.

subjects.label: Papal letters, oath withdrawals, and completed religious rupture
subjects.meaning: Pius VI’s March and April 1791 communications criticized the Civil Constitution and directed bishops against the oath; their publication caused retractions and anti-papal reaction.
subjects.stance: The author carefully notes that the texts stopped short of a simple formal condemnation, although all political actors treated them as decisive.

relationships.description: The letters converted earlier papal delay into an unmistakable political break.
Some sworn clergy withdrew after learning Rome’s position.
Popular hostility restricted the worship of refractories.

evidence.evidence_summary: Public release of the papal letters produced constitutional retractions, anti-papal demonstrations, obstruction of refractory worship, renewed Avignon debate, and the nuncio’s departure.
These linked developments are identified as completing the breach between revolutionary France and Rome.

subjects.label: Persecution of refractories and limits of religious liberty
subjects.meaning: Crowds and local activists obstructed nonjuror worship, attacked or threatened religious communities, and associated refractories with conspiracy.
subjects.stance: The author highlights the contradiction between declared freedom of worship and popular or official coercion against refractory Catholics.

relationships.description: The public papal break intensified anti-refractory hostility.
Coercion against worship displayed the collapse of the earlier rights consensus.
Persecution strengthened the religious basis of counter-revolution.

evidence.evidence_summary: Paris crowds prevented refractory clergy and congregations from exercising formally protected worship after the papal letters became public.
Popular action targeted refractory services and a convent, using intimidation and physical punishment.
The Varennes emergency renewed persecution by casting refractories as partners of aristocrats and foreign powers.

subjects.label: Religion as the popular base of counter-revolution
subjects.meaning: The religious schism transformed counter-revolution from an émigré and court project into a movement capable of mobilizing communities, clergy, and lay Catholics.
subjects.stance: The author makes religion—not aristocratic nostalgia—the first cause that gave counter-revolution wide moral legitimacy and social reach.

relationships.description: The oath forced religious allegiance into public political alignment.
Persecution made the constitutional order appear hostile to Catholic practice.
Jalès offered an early armed regional expression.
Émigré networks attempted to exploit popular religious unrest.

evidence.evidence_summary: Only after the papal rupture did counter-revolution acquire the beginnings of a broad constituency outside existing sectarian conflict zones.
Royal flight plans and improving royalist prospects are both connected to the same religious schism.
Varennes fears fused refractory clergy, aristocrats, and foreigners into an imagined national conspiracy.
The oath is judged to have supplied counter-revolutionaries with a higher cause than material self-interest.

subjects.label: Émigré royalist counter-revolution: Artois, Calonne, Lyons, and Koblenz
subjects.meaning: Artois and Calonne planned armed restoration from exile, linked agents to Catholic unrest, failed in the Rhône and at Jalès, and relocated the émigré court from Turin to Koblenz.
subjects.stance: The author depicts the network as unrealistic and insecure but increasingly connected to domestic religious conflict.

relationships.description: The network tried to harness newly popular religious counter-revolution.
Mirabeau sought to stop further Revolution without restoring aristocratic power.
Later noble and officer emigration greatly enlarged the exile problem.

evidence.evidence_summary: Artois and Calonne sought to rescue the monarchy and restore aristocratic power, using agents among Catholic leaders and planning a Rhône uprising.
Discovery of the Lyons papers and failure at Jalès exposed poor security and coordination.
Diplomatic embarrassment forced the émigré court from Turin; it re-established itself at Koblenz.

subjects.label: Mirabeau’s secret royal counsel
subjects.meaning: Mirabeau secretly advised and accepted payment from the crown while publicly retaining a radical reputation, advocating a strong monarchy and removal of the king from Paris.
subjects.stance: The author distinguishes his effort to arrest and stabilize the Revolution from émigré plans to reverse it and restore aristocratic authority.

relationships.description: His constitutional royalism was not émigré counter-revolution.
His death removed a major figure capable of mediating monarchy and Revolution.

evidence.evidence_summary: Mirabeau offered secret counsel and sought a stronger monarchy and a king outside Paris, but rejected the Turin émigrés’ restoration project.
Louis XVI ignored much of the advice, and Mirabeau died frustrated while his patriotic public reputation remained intact.

boundaries_and_exclusions: Do not treat payment alone as proof that Mirabeau shared the émigrés’ objective.

subjects.label: Army mutinies, Nancy, and General Bouillé
subjects.meaning: Conflict between aristocratic officers and politicized ranks produced mutinies, culminating in the Nancy rebellion and Bouillé’s violent repression.
subjects.stance: The author presents Bouillé’s action as temporarily restoring order while evoking ancien-régime despotism and making him appear dependable to the king.

relationships.description: The king’s confidence in Bouillé supported escape planning.
Military cohesion deteriorated further after Varennes and mass officer emigration.

evidence.evidence_summary: Mutinies spread through several garrisons as aristocratic command clashed with ranks influenced by the National Guard.
Bouillé stormed Nancy, executed mutineers, and imposed severe punishments; unrest subsided despite political outrage.
Bouillé later supplied the military plan and escorts for the royal flight.

subjects.label: Louis XVI’s religious alienation and decision to escape
subjects.meaning: The king’s misgivings over the Civil Constitution and oath deepened as clergy refused and Rome remained silent; family and devotional conflicts helped move him from passive resistance toward escape.
subjects.stance: The author assigns the religious schism a direct role in the king’s alienation while distinguishing the queen’s earlier rescue hopes from the king’s later independent decision.

relationships.description: The oath crisis reinforced the king’s religious estrangement.
Bouillé appeared to provide a reliable military partner.
The decision led to the flight to Varennes.

evidence.evidence_summary: Despite sanctioning the laws, the king rejected constitutional religious counsel and became more doubtful as clerical refusal spread.
His aunts’ refusal and departure for Rome sharpened the family conflict over the constitutional Church.
After the Saint-Cloud obstruction he regarded himself as a prisoner and began concrete preparations to leave.

subjects.label: Paris popular mobilization, women, the Cordeliers, and Lafayette
subjects.meaning: Women, popular newspapers, Jacobins, Cordeliers, and neighborhood societies drove anti-royal and anti-clerical demonstrations, while Lafayette repeatedly used the National Guard to contain them.
subjects.stance: The author presents Lafayette as caught between incompatible claims: self-appointed protector of monarchy, distrusted gaoler to royalists, and repressive enemy to popular activists.

relationships.description: The Day of Daggers dramatized elite and popular fears around royal security.
Saint-Cloud exposed the Guard’s unwillingness to clear the royal route.
The relationship between popular mobilization and coercion culminated at Champ de Mars.

evidence.evidence_summary: Women formed the core of demonstrations against suspected royal and clerical emigration, encouraged by radical clubs and newspapers.
Lafayette dispersed crowds but satisfied neither the royal family nor popular societies and could not reliably command his Guards.
At Champ de Mars Lafayette’s Guard eventually fired on a largely unarmed republican crowd.

subjects.label: Day of Daggers
subjects.meaning: Armed nobles entered the Tuileries while Lafayette was suppressing a crowd at Vincennes, producing suspicions of an escape attempt and mass disarmament in the palace.
subjects.stance: The author treats the incident as a revealing security panic rather than proof of an actual royal escape plan.

relationships.description: The incident exposed Lafayette’s precarious role between court and street.
It contributed to escalating suspicion before the Saint-Cloud crisis.

evidence.evidence_summary: The simultaneous Vincennes crowd and armed convergence on the Tuileries made Lafayette rush back and disarm royalist nobles.

boundaries_and_exclusions: Do not assert that the incident was an authenticated royal escape operation.

subjects.label: Saint-Cloud incident and the king’s sense of captivity
subjects.meaning: After Louis XVI received communion from a refractory priest, a crowd and insubordinate National Guards prevented the royal family from leaving Paris for Easter at Saint-Cloud.
subjects.stance: The author finds no evidence that this excursion was itself an escape, but treats the obstruction as the decisive experience that convinced the king he was a prisoner.

relationships.description: Religious alignment made the king’s Easter plans politically explosive.
The experience of captivity accelerated the Varennes project.

evidence.evidence_summary: A crowd immobilized the royal carriage after news of refractory communion, and National Guards refused Lafayette’s order to clear the route.
Although not demonstrated to be an escape attempt, the episode made rumors self-reinforcing and prompted concrete royal flight preparations.

subjects.label: Paris unemployment, prices, assignat depreciation, and social pressure
subjects.meaning: Loss of luxury employment, closure of religious establishments, stagnant wages, and rising prices under depreciating assignats created a volatile urban setting.
subjects.stance: The author links economic distress to popular activism without reducing political mobilization to subsistence grievance alone.

relationships.description: Economic pressure encouraged wage organization after guild abolition.
Material distress formed part of the setting for Paris popular mobilization.

evidence.evidence_summary: Noble retrenchment and closure of religious institutions displaced servants and luxury workers as anti-clerical agitation intensified.
Charity workshops absorbed some labor, wages remained weak, and assignat depreciation contributed to price pressure and coin scarcity.

subjects.label: Guild abolition, worker coalition, and the Le Chapelier Law
subjects.meaning: After abolition of trade corporations, workers organized for higher wages and collective action; the Assembly responded by prohibiting worker organizations, concerted industrial action, and official recognition.
subjects.stance: The author emphasizes the law’s origin in revolutionary anti-corporatism and its durable restriction of labor organization, while noting that its sponsor had become a consolidating moderate.

relationships.description: Urban labor pressure and price conditions gave collective wage action urgency.
Le Chapelier’s sponsorship embodied the shift from radical reform to constitutional consolidation.

evidence.evidence_summary: Guild abolition removed both privilege and employers’ coordination, while carpenters and blacksmiths threatened broad wage action.
The June law prohibited worker organizations, collective industrial action, petitions from such bodies, and public employment of their members.
The restriction is identified as governing French industrial relations for seventy-three years.

subjects.label: Moderation of revolutionary leaders and the Triumvirate
subjects.meaning: Le Chapelier, Barnave, Duport, and the Lameths moved from radical leadership toward consolidation, preservation of monarchy, and control of popular pressure.
subjects.stance: The author attributes moderation to fear of constitutional collapse and popular escalation, but also to calculations about post-Constituent power.

relationships.description: Robespierre rose as former radical leaders moved to the center.
The monarchist secession created the Feuillant organization.
Moderates shaped the final constitutional settlement.

evidence.evidence_summary: Former radicals concluded that further Revolution threatened existing gains and that the constitution needed completion and implementation.
Barnave, Duport, and the Lameths moderated out of concern for the monarchy’s constitutional role and their own future political influence.
Their move to the center elevated a smaller left opposition around Robespierre.
After Champ de Mars the triumvirate cooperated with Lafayette on final constitutional revision.

subjects.label: Robespierre’s rise and the ‘thirty voices’
subjects.meaning: The moderation of former leaders opened space for Robespierre and a small left group; his incorruptible image, Jacobin activity, and procedural victories increased his influence.
subjects.stance: The author records contemporary perceptions of republican conviction but explicitly doubts whether Robespierre openly held a republican position at this stage.

relationships.description: Moderation and fragmentation opened political space on the left.
His exclusion motions reshaped later revolutionary leadership.
He supported antislavery and equal political rights in the colonial debate.
He was among the few deputies remaining with the Jacobins after the Feuillant split.

evidence.evidence_summary: The triumvirate’s move toward the center brought Robespierre and a small left group to prominence.
Contemporaries saw principled republican tendencies and predicted his rise, although he denied republicanism and the author treats the classification as uncertain.
He increasingly dominated the Jacobins and won election as public prosecutor.

boundaries_and_exclusions: Preserve the author’s uncertainty about whether Robespierre was already a republican.

subjects.label: Robespierre’s self-denying ordinances
subjects.meaning: Robespierre secured rules barring Constituent deputies from executive office for four years and excluding them from the next Legislative Assembly.
subjects.stance: The author regards the measures as profoundly consequential in retrospect while explaining that contemporaries often saw them as tactical blows against rivals.

relationships.description: The motions were Robespierre’s first tangible national successes.
Excluding experienced deputies shaped the personnel available to operate the new constitutional system.

evidence.evidence_summary: The April motion barred deputies from near-term executive office, and the May motion excluded Constituent members from the next legislature.
Right-wing tactical support helped pass measures whose long-term effects exceeded their immediate factional meaning.

subjects.label: Saint-Domingue: slavery and political rights for free people of color
subjects.meaning: The Assembly preserved slavery in 1790, then confronted white colonial resistance to political rights for free people of color; Robespierre successfully argued for rights irrespective of color.
subjects.stance: The author emphasizes the contradiction between universal rights language and racial exclusion, while distinguishing emancipation from the narrower but contested question of free-colored citizenship.

relationships.description: The colonial settlement exposed exclusions within the Constituent Assembly’s rights achievement.
Victory in the debate contributed to Robespierre’s growing standing.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Assembly declined to abolish slavery, revealing limits in its application of the Rights of Man.
White colonists violently resisted free-colored claims; Barnave warned against concessions while Robespierre opposed slavery and won political rights regardless of color.

subjects.label: Flight to Varennes
subjects.meaning: Louis XVI and his family attempted to leave Paris for the eastern frontier under arrangements made through Fersen and Bouillé, but delays, public suspicion, and recognition led to their arrest at Varennes.
subjects.stance: The author identifies Varennes as the Revolution’s second great turning point, exposing the king’s rejection of the settlement and forcing choices over monarchy, republicanism, and war.

relationships.description: Religious and political alienation moved the king toward escape.
Bouillé supplied the military component.
The manifesto disclosed the king’s constitutional objections.
The Assembly suspended the king while preserving monarchy.
Republican politics became public and organized.

evidence.evidence_summary: Fersen arranged the route and Bouillé the escorts toward Montmédy; delays and suspicious troop movements undermined secrecy.
Recognition at Sainte-Ménehould and Drouet’s warning enabled Varennes to stop the royal party before military rescue.
The failure postponed immediate war but made the monarch’s repudiation of the Revolution impossible to ignore.
Like the clerical oath, Varennes is judged a turning point because it compelled political choices most actors had avoided.

subjects.label: Louis XVI’s Varennes manifesto and repudiation of the Revolution
subjects.meaning: The king’s proclamation denounced captivity, property violations, anarchy, Jacobin power, deviation from the cahiers, weakness of the crown, and implicitly the religious settlement.
subjects.stance: The author treats the manifesto as clear evidence that the king had renounced the Revolution, regardless of uncertainty over his intended destination after Montmédy.

relationships.description: The manifesto was left behind during the flight.
The Assembly publicly treated the king as kidnapped and blamed advisers.
It made the later constitutional acceptance lack credibility.

evidence.evidence_summary: The king concentrated on a manifesto rejecting the post-October settlement while flight arrangements were prepared.
The document enumerated political, constitutional, property, public-order, club, and religious objections to the revolutionary regime.
The closing assessment contrasts the manifesto and flight with later claims that royal acceptance of the Constitution was sincere.

boundaries_and_exclusions: Retain the source’s uncertainty over whether the king planned only remote negotiation or foreign-backed return.

subjects.label: Assembly response to Varennes: kidnapping fiction, suspension, and retention of monarchy
subjects.meaning: The Constituent Assembly governed without the king, suspended his functions, blamed Bouillé and advisers, and publicly pretended that the monarch had been abducted so the nearly completed monarchy-centered constitution could survive.
subjects.stance: The author calls the account a conscious fiction driven by fear of regency, constitutional redrafting, and empowered popular republican forces.

relationships.description: The policy contained the immediate constitutional crisis caused by the flight.
Republican petitions rejected restoration without national consent.
Preserving the crown allowed final Feuillant constitutional revision.

evidence.evidence_summary: The crisis demonstrated that ministers, military administration, and debate could continue without an active monarch.
Most deputies nevertheless rejected deposition and adopted the kidnapping explanation to avoid reopening the constitution.
The Assembly retained monarchy, controlled the executive, and assigned blame to Bouillé and associates who had already escaped.

subjects.label: Varennes emergency, vigilance, and the Jacobin network
subjects.meaning: The royal flight produced nationwide expectations of Austrian intervention, Guard mobilization, vigilance committees, attacks on refractories, and intense political-club participation.
subjects.stance: The author shows that the same Jacobin network strengthened by the religious crisis now struggled to reconcile outrage at the king with limited support for a republic.

relationships.description: The failed flight generated the emergency.
The already extensive club network supplied the machinery of vigilance.
Cordeliers and Social Circle activists organized a republican petition.

evidence.evidence_summary: Communities mobilized Guards and committees under expectations of invasion and linked refractory clergy to aristocratic and foreign conspiracy.
Club membership surged, many affiliates demanded trial or deposition, but relatively few endorsed republican government.
The Paris Jacobins’ inability to resolve the monarchy question opened the club to external radical pressure.

subjects.label: Republican movement, Cordeliers, and Social Circle petition
subjects.meaning: Varennes brought republicanism into open politics as the Cordeliers and Social Circle demanded deposition or national consultation and drafted a petition treating the crown as vacant.
subjects.stance: The author distinguishes mass anger and anti-restoration demands from uniformly settled republican doctrine, which remained limited even in the Jacobins.

relationships.description: The flight converted latent suspicion into overt republican organization.
Support for the petition divided the Jacobins and prompted the Feuillant secession.
The signing campaign at Champ de Mars ended in massacre and repression.

evidence.evidence_summary: Royal symbols were attacked and the Cordeliers led a mass petition for deposition or a national referendum.
The Social Circle and Cordeliers pressed the Jacobins to oppose reinstatement and organized a petitioning campaign.
The final petition declared an effective abdication and conditioned any replacement on national consent, making it functionally republican.

subjects.label: Jacobin–Feuillant split
subjects.meaning: Committed constitutional monarchists, including Lafayette and the triumvirate, left the Jacobins after the anti-restoration petition and founded a rival Society of the Friends of the Constitution at the Feuillants.
subjects.stance: The author presents the split as organizational consolidation of the monarchist–republican divide, although Robespierre’s Jacobin rump withdrew support for the petition.
acceptable_access: Society of the Friends of the Constitution—division
anticipated_reader_lookup_routes: Society of the Friends of the Constitution—division

relationships.description: The republican-leaning petition made coexistence in the Paris club untenable.
Moderate former radicals acquired a distinct institutional base.
The Feuillants led the final constitutional settlement.
Their weak provincial and right-wing support exposed the settlement’s narrow base.

evidence.evidence_summary: Most active Jacobins and nearly all deputies seceded to the Feuillants, leaving Robespierre, Pétion, and a few allies behind.
Robespierre persuaded the rump to withdraw from the petition, but the Cordeliers proceeded and the institutional rupture remained.
Only a small minority of provincial affiliates permanently followed the Feuillants, limiting their national organizational success.

subjects.label: Champ de Mars massacre and repression of the popular republican movement
subjects.meaning: National Guards under Lafayette fired on a mass petitioning crowd at Champ de Mars after martial law was declared, killing dozens and initiating arrests and suppression of radical clubs and newspapers.
subjects.stance: The author treats the massacre as the temporary crushing of an emerging republican movement and as the coercive condition enabling conservative constitutional completion.

relationships.description: The petition campaign brought the republican question to a mass public confrontation.
Lafayette and the National Guard enforced martial law.
Repression cleared the political field for final Feuillant amendments.

evidence.evidence_summary: Tens of thousands gathered and thousands signed before lynchings supplied the mayor’s justification for martial law.
The Guard answered stones and some shots with fire on a largely unarmed crowd, killing roughly fifty.
Arrests, flight and concealment of activists, shuttered newspapers, and inactive clubs temporarily shattered organized republican pressure.
The Assembly then completed constitutional revision without comparable street opposition.

subjects.label: Feuillant constitutional settlement and conservative consolidation
subjects.meaning: After Champ de Mars, Lafayette and moderate deputies revised and completed the Constitution while seeking to reconcile the king, restrict popular pressure, and place government in propertied hands.
subjects.stance: The author recognizes limited concessions but interprets the settlement as a conservative consolidation that left the monarchy’s basic 1789 architecture intact and failed to resolve religion or legitimacy.

relationships.description: Suppression of popular republicanism reduced immediate opposition.
Electoral design concentrated decisive power among wealthy landowners.
Press restrictions sought to curb popular political agitation.
The settlement culminated in royal acceptance and the Constituent’s dissolution.
It failed to attract the right, most clubs, the king’s trust, or popular republicans.

evidence.evidence_summary: The massacre’s aftermath allowed Lafayette and the triumvirate to cooperate on a definitive constitutional text.
Amendments separated the Civil Constitution from the constitutional oath, rejected extreme anti-refractory measures, altered electoral rules, and restricted the press.
More ambitious monarchist proposals for an absolute veto, ministers in the Assembly, and a second chamber were not revived.
The Feuillants declared the Revolution complete when the king accepted, despite unresolved religious and republican divisions.

subjects.label: Electoral qualifications and concealed oligarchic control
subjects.meaning: The Assembly removed the visible silver-mark qualification for deputies while raising the wealth threshold for secondary electors who actually chose them.
subjects.stance: The author calls the reform disingenuous because it appeared to democratize eligibility while placing decisive electoral leverage more securely with wealthy landowners.

relationships.description: The change was a key conservative amendment in the Feuillant settlement.
It limits universalist claims made for the Constituent Assembly’s constitutional achievement.

evidence.evidence_summary: The formal deputy property test was abolished, but the qualification for secondary electors was raised above it.
The change came after the next legislature’s elections, whose successful candidates had already met the earlier qualification.

subjects.label: Press restriction of August 1791
subjects.meaning: The Assembly authorized prosecution for writing that deliberately encouraged disobedience, contempt for authorities, or resistance and allowed officials to sue over attacks on their probity.
subjects.stance: The author presents the law as a Feuillant attempt to suppress the popular political energy blamed for the spring and summer crises.

relationships.description: Press control formed part of conservative constitutional consolidation.
The measure followed repression of radical newspapers and clubs after Champ de Mars.

evidence.evidence_summary: The law criminalized defined forms of anti-authority advocacy and expanded civil remedies for public officials.
Robespierre stood nearly alone against a measure promoted as a safeguard after popular unrest.

subjects.label: Émigré legislation, officer exodus, and collapse of army discipline
subjects.meaning: The Assembly imposed return deadlines, taxation, and official lists on émigrés, while Varennes and a reordered military oath accelerated the departure of nobles and thousands of officers and deepened mutiny.
subjects.stance: The author treats emigration as both a failed target of legislation and a major institutional threat, not simply elite political symbolism.

relationships.description: The growing exodus transformed the scale of émigré counter-revolution.
A crumbling army made foreign intervention rumors more threatening.
Elite withdrawal deprived the Constitution of potential support.

evidence.evidence_summary: The first effective émigré law required return, threatened triple taxation, and initiated official lists.
Varennes and the new loyalty oath helped drive perhaps six thousand officers—over half the corps—abroad.
Later repeal and general amnesty did not reverse the flow, while renewed mutinies left army discipline near collapse.
The chapter closes with many nobles withdrawn internally or across the Rhine, further weakening the constitutional order.

subjects.label: Foreign intervention fears and the Declaration of Pillnitz
subjects.meaning: Varennes encouraged expectations that Austria and Prussia would intervene; Leopold’s Padua Circular and the Pillnitz declaration invoked common monarchical interest and conditional action.
subjects.stance: The author distinguishes diplomatic reality from French perception: Austria did not plan an immediate crusade, but émigré involvement and provocative wording made the declaration politically inflammatory.

relationships.description: Varennes made foreign rescue appear imminent.
Army weakness magnified perceived external threat.
War rumors helped keep politics divided despite Feuillant conciliation.

evidence.evidence_summary: Rumors of a foreign-backed émigré invasion persisted as Leopold appealed for coordinated monarchical action and Prussia responded.
Pillnitz described the king’s position as a European concern and offered conditional common action.
Austria privately viewed intervention as unlikely, yet émigré sponsorship and accompanying appeals made the declaration needlessly provocative.
Foreign-war rumors framed both the Assembly’s final days and annexation of the papal enclaves.

subjects.label: Constitution of 1791: acceptance and Constituent Assembly legacy
subjects.meaning: Louis XVI accepted the completed Constitution amid amnesty and celebration, and the Constituent Assembly ended after dismantling the ancien régime and establishing enduring principles and institutions.
subjects.stance: The author credits the Assembly’s enormous structural achievement while insisting that its own policies also planted the religious, royal, republican, colonial, and social contradictions that threatened the new order.

relationships.description: Feuillant revision supplied the final political form.
Colonial exclusion contradicted universal rights claims.
The king’s earlier manifesto made acceptance suspect.
Institutional achievement did not equal political viability.

evidence.evidence_summary: The king accepted the completed Constitution, amnesty accompanied promulgation, and the Feuillants proclaimed ordinary constitutional life.
The Assembly is credited with dismantling the old regime and establishing principles and structures of lasting importance.
The same conclusion assigns the Assembly responsibility for coercive religious division and the seeds of later radicalization.
The closing prediction denies the Constitution a stable body of supporters.

subjects.label: Feuillant failure and fragility of the constitutional monarchy
subjects.meaning: The Feuillants failed to win royalists, most provincial clubs, major Paris newspapers, or the radical popular movement; war rumors, religious division, émigré hostility, and royal bad faith persisted.
subjects.stance: The author’s final judgment is not merely that the settlement faced opposition, but that it lacked genuine friends across the political field.

relationships.description: Conservative constitutional consolidation did not generate consent.
The accumulated fractures of 1790–1791 made stability unlikely.
Noble and officer withdrawal removed elite support.
External-threat politics kept factions polarized.

evidence.evidence_summary: Right-wing elites withheld support, most provincial clubs remained Jacobin, and no major Paris paper adopted the Feuillant cause.
Foreign-war rumors and émigré intrigue preserved polarization despite attempts at conciliation.
Religious schism, royal insincerity, republican growth, and noble withdrawal survived the Constitution’s promulgation.
The chapter ends by endorsing the contemporary judgment that the new Constitution had no durable constituency.

subjects.label: National Assembly Ecclesiastical Committee
subjects.meaning: The committee that designed comprehensive Church reform acquired a stronger lay majority when clerical members resisted the breadth of proposed change.
subjects.stance: The author distinguishes a small freethinking minority from the larger group of sincere Catholic reformers, preventing the committee from being reduced to simple anti-religious intent.
acceptable_access: Ecclesiastical Committee of the National Assembly
anticipated_reader_lookup_routes: Ecclesiastical Committee of the National Assembly

relationships.description: The committee produced the Civil Constitution.
Its composition and reasoning expressed national-Church sovereignty.

evidence.evidence_summary: Additional lay members were added when clerical resistance slowed the original committee’s work.
Most members sought a reformed Catholic Church, although a minority drew directly on Enlightenment anti-clericalism.

subjects.label: Confiscation and sale of Church lands
subjects.meaning: The nation seized ecclesiastical estates, inventoried them, and prepared their sale while taking responsibility for charitable and educational functions.
subjects.stance: The author treats confiscation as both a fiscal and constitutional transformation whose local enforcement helped polarize religion.

relationships.description: Confiscation removed the Church’s remaining independent resources.
Monastic inventories helped provoke the Montauban riot.
State ownership underpinned the salaried national Church.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Assembly confiscated Church estates and promised to assume public functions previously supported by them.
Inventories and sales proceeded nationwide while religious houses were being closed.
Acceptance of land inventories and the Civil Constitution became public tests of revolutionary loyalty.

subjects.label: Salaried clergy and state responsibility for Church functions
subjects.meaning: After taking ecclesiastical property, the nation promised salaries to clergy and assumed responsibility for education and charity, making the Church materially dependent on the state.
subjects.stance: The author notes that salary reform benefited poorly paid priests but reduced other incomes and created uncertainty over when payment would begin.

relationships.description: Nationalization transferred both resources and obligations to the state.
Public salaries were part of the Civil Constitution’s organization.

evidence.evidence_summary: Deputies promised state support for education, charity, and a substantial minimum parish salary, but many clergy faced cuts or delayed payment.
The Civil Constitution formalized relatively generous salary scales while redistributing income away from many bishops and rectors.

subjects.label: Richerism and representative Church government
subjects.meaning: Richerist traditions favored election and priestly synods as checks on episcopal hierarchy, influencing advisory councils in the Civil Constitution.
subjects.stance: The author limits the analogy: Richerists did not advocate unrestricted lay election by religiously mixed citizen bodies.

relationships.description: Richerism supplied a partial precedent for less hierarchical appointments.
It supported some reform but not the full electoral mechanism.

evidence.evidence_summary: The episcopal advisory council echoed Richerist arguments for elected and synodal government, but the law went beyond them in empowering lay voters.

subjects.label: Constitutional clergy
subjects.meaning: Clergy who swore the oath staffed the reorganized national Church, gained new avenues of promotion, and faced contested legitimacy after papal intervention.
subjects.stance: The author treats constitutional clergy as a real institutional constituency rather than merely compliant opportunists, while noting withdrawals and staffing weakness.

relationships.description: The oath publicly defined constitutional clergy.
They supplied personnel for the Civil Constitution.
Refractories refused the oath and retained competing religious authority.

evidence.evidence_summary: Sworn clergy, former regulars, and low-status priests gained access to benefices and episcopal advancement.
Publication of the papal position led a significant minority of jurors to retract.
In Paris, popular crowds strongly favored priests who accepted the new order.

subjects.label: Refractory clergy
subjects.meaning: Nonjurors rejected the oath and often retained strong parish support, becoming a large, geographically concentrated body whose worship and political loyalty were contested.
subjects.stance: The author rejects the Assembly’s expectation of a tiny episcopal faction and shows refractories as central to popular opposition and counter-revolution.

relationships.description: Refusal to swear created the refractory category.
Their worship and congregations faced coercion.
Their community standing helped religious counter-revolution acquire depth.

evidence.evidence_summary: Around half the clergy refused despite public pressure and the Assembly’s expectation of only limited dissent.
Refusal was especially strong in the west, border regions, and many provincial cities, often reflecting parish solidarity.
Staffing shortages forced the Assembly to retain some refractories temporarily.
After Varennes they were widely suspected of joining aristocratic and foreign conspiracy.

subjects.label: National Guard as a contested revolutionary force
subjects.meaning: National Guard units enforced policy, embodied local sectarian alignments, influenced regular soldiers, and proved unreliable when asked to coerce politically sympathetic crowds.
subjects.stance: The author presents no uniform Guard: units could be Protestant, Catholic, counter-revolutionary, royal-protective, mutinous in sympathy, or repressive according to place and crisis.

relationships.description: Guard control carried sectarian political power.
Lafayette depended on the Paris Guard for order.
Its coercive action made the massacre possible.

evidence.evidence_summary: Militia control was central to Catholic–Protestant conflict in Nîmes and Montauban.
A Guard federation could be redirected toward counter-revolution, as at Jalès.
Guard egalitarianism influenced regular ranks and aggravated conflict with aristocratic officers.
Paris Guards refused Lafayette’s order to clear the king’s route to Saint-Cloud.
At Champ de Mars Guards under Lafayette fired on the petitioning crowd.

subjects.label: Women in religious and popular political action
subjects.meaning: Women led or sustained crowd action in both Catholic resistance and Parisian revolutionary mobilization.
subjects.stance: The author treats women as active political agents and, in Paris, as the mainstay of popular demonstrations rather than incidental participants.

relationships.description: Women played a leading role in the Montauban riot.
Women were central to Paris popular mobilization.
Women helped enforce popular hostility to refractory worship.

evidence.evidence_summary: Devout women led the Montauban crowd that blocked monastic inventories and attacked the militia.
Women sustained Paris demonstrations against suspected emigration and refractory practice, including direct coercion of a convent.

subjects.label: Cordeliers Club
subjects.meaning: The Society of the Friends of the Rights of Man fostered popular societies, supported anti-royal mobilization, demanded deposition or national consultation after Varennes, and continued the republican petition after the Jacobins withdrew.
subjects.stance: The author makes the Cordeliers a distinct driver of popular republican politics, not merely a radical wing of the Jacobins.
acceptable_access: Society of the Friends of the Rights of Man
anticipated_reader_lookup_routes: Society of the Friends of the Rights of Man

relationships.description: The club was a principal institution of the emerging republican movement.
It worked with the Social Circle on anti-restoration politics.
Repression after Champ de Mars stopped its meetings.

evidence.evidence_summary: The Cordeliers encouraged popular societies and anti-royal demonstrations while defining itself around rights rather than the existing Constitution.
After Varennes it delivered a mass-backed petition demanding deposition or a referendum.
It carried forward the Champ de Mars petition when the Jacobins withdrew support.

subjects.label: Social Circle
subjects.meaning: A Paris club known before Varennes for utopian discussion became an organizer and publisher of republican opposition through the Bouche de fer and mass intervention at the Jacobins.
subjects.stance: The author treats Varennes as transforming the Circle into an important but short-lived republican mobilizer.

relationships.description: The Circle supplied publication and crowd organization to the republican campaign.
It partnered with the Cordeliers.
Champ de Mars repression destroyed the club.

evidence.evidence_summary: Brissot’s newspaper and Social Circle activity helped establish his democratic reputation.
After Varennes the Circle cooperated with the Cordeliers, publicized their petition, and brought thousands into the Jacobin meeting.
Its newspaper issued the anti-restoration petition, but post-massacre repression ended the organization permanently.

subjects.label: Lafayette in the crisis of 1791
subjects.meaning: Lafayette sought to protect constitutional royalty and public order through the National Guard but lost trust among royalists, radicals, and sometimes his own men.
subjects.stance: The author portrays him as politically isolated: court supporters saw a gaoler, popular societies a repressor, and events repeatedly exposed his limited command.

relationships.description: His political position depended on the Paris National Guard.
His force carried out Champ de Mars repression.
He joined the Feuillant split.
He collaborated in final revision.

evidence.evidence_summary: Lafayette dispersed anti-royal and anti-clerical crowds yet earned neither royal gratitude nor popular legitimacy.
The Day of Daggers and Saint-Cloud incidents exposed his inability to guarantee royal freedom or fully control the Guard.
He led the force that fired at Champ de Mars and joined the Feuillant secession.
After the massacre he cooperated with former rivals to complete constitutional revision.

subjects.label: Monarchical Club
subjects.meaning: Former monarchiens founded a rival club to challenge the Jacobins, but its subsidized bread campaign enabled opponents to have it closed for market disruption.
subjects.stance: The author treats the club as evidence of a temporary conservative opening whose tactics undermined its legitimacy.

relationships.description: The club anticipated the turn toward consolidation.
It attempted unsuccessfully to compete with the Jacobins.

evidence.evidence_summary: Former monarchiens built a large rival club as political moderation gathered momentum.
Its heavily subsidized bread sales invited Jacobin attack and official closure for disrupting the market.

subjects.label: Barnave’s political trajectory
subjects.meaning: Barnave moved from Protestant-linked radical leadership and Jacobin prominence through defense of colonial order to constitutional moderation, royal conciliation, and Feuillant leadership.
subjects.stance: The author treats the shift as both strategic and constitutional, intensified by fear that royal flight would destroy the system.

relationships.description: Barnave was a leading member of the triumvirate.
His colonial position contrasted with Robespierre’s.
He became a Feuillant leader.
He led constitutional conciliation.

evidence.evidence_summary: Barnave appears among prominent Protestant radical leaders whose identity fed Catholic suspicions.
He led patriotic efforts to pressure clerical deputies toward the oath.
By early summer he and the triumvirate were moderating to preserve monarchy and future influence.
He defended slavery and warned against free-colored political claims before Robespierre defeated his position.
After escorting the royal family from Varennes, he led efforts to reconcile the king through constitutional amendment.

subjects.label: Preservation of slavery in Saint-Domingue
subjects.meaning: The Constituent Assembly declined to abolish colonial slavery in March 1790 despite its universal rights language.
subjects.stance: The author explicitly presents this as a limit and contradiction in the Revolution’s application of the Rights of Man.

relationships.description: This separates slavery from the free-colored citizenship debate.
Racial exclusion qualified the Assembly’s universalist legacy.

evidence.evidence_summary: Following Barnave’s committee recommendation, the Assembly preserved slavery in the colony.
The decision demonstrates that the rights settlement did not extend equally to enslaved Black people.

subjects.label: Political rights of free people of color in Saint-Domingue
subjects.meaning: Free people of color demanded political rights against determined white colonial resistance and violent repression; the Assembly ultimately granted rights regardless of color.
subjects.stance: The author distinguishes this citizenship contest from abolition and credits Robespierre with defeating Barnave’s opposition.

relationships.description: This is the citizenship branch of the colonial debate.
Political rights for free people did not abolish slavery.
The victory contributed to Robespierre’s rise.

evidence.evidence_summary: White colonists resisted free-colored political claims and brutally suppressed an armed assertion in 1790.
Robespierre’s equality argument prevailed over Barnave’s warnings, granting political rights without a color bar.

subjects.label: Émigré legislation of 1791
subjects.meaning: The Assembly ordered émigrés home, imposed triple taxation, and created official lists, before later repealing the law in an amnesty.
subjects.stance: The author presents the policy as a late and ineffective attempt to contain a rapidly growing political and military exodus.

relationships.description: This isolates the legal response to emigration.
Officer flight continued despite legislation.

evidence.evidence_summary: The July law required return within a month, threatened triple tax, and created official lists after earlier proposals had failed.
The September repeal and amnesty did not stop the expanding departure of officers and nobles.
Émigré princes continued to influence international threats and constitutional acceptance from abroad.

subjects.label: Emigration of the army officer corps
subjects.meaning: A reordered loyalty oath and the Varennes débâcle accelerated the departure of roughly six thousand officers, more than half the corps.
subjects.stance: The author treats the exodus as a severe institutional loss that also strengthened external counter-revolution.

relationships.description: This isolates the military personnel crisis.
Departing officers enlarged the émigré counter-revolution.
Loss of leadership worsened military disorder.

evidence.evidence_summary: The new loyalty formula and outrage over Varennes alienated aristocratic officers.
Bouillé’s departure was followed by an estimated six thousand officers, over half the army’s officer corps.
Even officers inclined to remain were pushed out as discipline and trust collapsed.

subjects.label: Count d’Artois and émigré restoration plans
subjects.meaning: From exile, Artois pursued military restoration intended to free Louis XVI and undo revolutionary change, used Calonne’s advice, and cultivated domestic Catholic resistance despite royal objections.
subjects.stance: The author portrays him as unrealistic but persistent and distinguishes his restoration project from constitutional royalism.

relationships.description: Artois was central to the émigré network.
Mirabeau rejected restoration of aristocratic power.
His agents exploited Catholic unrest at Jalès.

evidence.evidence_summary: Agents of Artois connected with Jalès organizers while he imagined armed rescue and revolutionary reversal.
He increasingly followed Calonne and sought a Rhône-wide rising despite limited royal cooperation.
Louis XVI asked him to abandon the Lyons plan, and diplomatic pressure later displaced his court from Turin.
Near constitutional completion the king again urged Artois to return and stop plotting.

subjects.label: Martial law and the red flag at Champ de Mars
subjects.meaning: Paris authorities invoked the October 1789 martial-law decree after lynchings at the petition site, then advanced under the red warning flag before the Guard fired.
subjects.stance: The author presents the legal invocation as the immediate mechanism of repression while making clear that the crowd was largely unarmed and the response disproportionate.

relationships.description: Martial law framed the massacre and repression.
Lafayette led the Guard under the declaration.

evidence.evidence_summary: Mayor Bailly used the earlier decree and two lynchings to declare martial law at the mass petition.
The Guard displayed the red warning flag, encountered stones and some gunfire, and then shot into a largely unarmed crowd.

subjects.label: General amnesty and constitutional promulgation
subjects.meaning: A general amnesty accompanied promulgation of the Constitution, repealing the recent anti-emigration law and symbolizing the Feuillant hope for reconciliation.
subjects.stance: The author shows that formal amnesty did not reverse emigration, religious division, or distrust of the king.

relationships.description: Amnesty marked constitutional promulgation.
It did not stop emigration or restore military cohesion.
It embodied Feuillant reconciliation.

evidence.evidence_summary: The September amnesty repealed the new emigration penalties but failed to halt officer departure.
Amnesty and public rejoicing accompanied royal acceptance, even as deep political divisions remained.

exclusions.decision: No CHUNK-006 subject evidence was assigned to context pages; they were read only to establish boundaries and continuity.
Observers, quoted correspondents, and minor participants mentioned only to supply testimony were not promoted to independent subjects.
examples: W. A. Miles as quotation source

exclusions.decision: Drouet and Fersen remain access terms within the Varennes subject rather than separate biographies because the chapter treats their operational roles briefly.
Individual sees, parishes, clergy, and local clubs used only as examples of broader patterns were not automatically promoted.
Absent endnotes and other missing back matter were excluded from discovery and word-count denominators rather than treated as omissions.
No raw extracted text, exact quotation field, or extended source passage is retained; evidence summaries are short page-specific paraphrases.
Density calibration was not used as a quota, minimum, ceiling, pruning rule, or padding instruction.

uncertainties.issue: Whether Robespierre was already privately or publicly republican in early 1791.
alternatives: Not yet republican or not demonstrably so
uncertainties.source_position: The chapter explicitly doubts the label while reporting contemporary testimony that inferred republican conviction.

uncertainties.issue: Louis XVI’s intended course after reaching Montmédy.
alternatives: Negotiate from a secure French position
Emigrate and return with foreign military backing
uncertainties.source_position: The chapter leaves intention unresolved but judges either course a fundamental challenge to the revolutionary settlement.

uncertainties.issue: Whether the Day of Daggers was an actual escape plot.
alternatives: Royalist security response interpreted as an escape plot
uncertainties.source_position: The episode is presented as appearing to be a plot without a definitive finding.

uncertainties.issue: Whether the planned Saint-Cloud excursion was itself an escape attempt.
uncertainties.source_position: The chapter says evidence does not support treating the excursion as an escape plan.

uncertainties.issue: Exact indexable word count under alternative editorial tokenization conventions.
alternatives: A slightly different total if hyphenated compounds or typographic artifacts are counted differently
uncertainties.source_position: The recorded count is reproducible and suitable as the frozen denominator when its method is retained.

selection_method.unit: independently searchable source subject rather than a proposed finished-index heading
principles: Retain principal subjects and significant localized or subsidiary subjects even when confined to one passage.
Split or add direct-access records when a scholarly reader could plausibly seek one component without the related umbrella.
Retain named people, institutions, laws, and events only when the chapter analyzes them, assigns them a material causal or institutional role, or makes them independently useful.
Preserve broader conceptual records alongside specific access records when the source supplies both a chapter-level explanation and independently retrievable components.
Treat all chunk-level priorities as provisional until whole-source benchmark synthesis.
Use optional only for defensible supplemental access whose absence would not materially reduce usefulness.
Do not use density calibration to set the subject count or priority.

limitations: The supplied source begins with body page 1 and omits front matter, notes/endnotes, bibliography, and publisher index; unavailable matter was neither reviewed nor counted.
CHUNK-006 owns only document/source pages 136–158. Cross-chapter consolidation and final global priorities remain the responsibility of source-benchmark synthesis.
Named-person granularity follows independent scholarly retrieval value in this chapter; minor witnesses and examples remain embedded access terms or exclusions.
